narrative:
The model predicted a 52% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that mattered most to the decision were your undergraduate grades, your performance in the third year of law school, and your family income. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were admitted, signaling that your later-law-school performance raised serious concern about passing the bar. 

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 actually worked in your favor; it is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. Your low family income also pulled the prediction downward, away from failure. Even so, these two positive influences were not enough to overcome the negative signal from your third-year ranking.

Because the model’s decision rested so heavily on that single weak year, the clearest next step is to strengthen your academic record. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or waiting until you have stronger recent grades before reapplying. Improving that later performance record is the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
